canonicalExplanation.summary: Like C, each `.cpp` file is a **translation unit**: preprocessed, compiled to an object file, then **linked**. C++ adds two big rules. The **One Definition Rule (ODR)**: each non-inline function or variable has exactly one definition in the program, and things that may appear in several units (classes, inline functions, templates) must be **identical** everywhere. And **templates** are blueprints, not code: the compiler only generates `max<int>` in a unit that can **see the full template definition**. So template definitions normally live in **headers**; put one in a .cpp file and other units get `undefined reference` link errors.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner declares `template <typename T> T biggest(T a, T b);` in util.h and defines it in util.cpp. main.cpp calls biggest(3, 7), every file compiles, and the link fails with `undefined reference to int biggest<int>(int, int)`. A template definition remains visible in a header so a translation unit can instantiate it for int before linking. In this lesson you'll classify and repair preprocessing, compilation and linking failures.

examples.title: A template that must live in the header
examples.situation: A template definition remains visible in a header so a translation unit can instantiate it for int before linking.
walkthrough: **A template definition remains visible in a header:** biggest's body moves from util.cpp into util.h.
**So a translation unit can instantiate it for int:** main.cpp generates biggest<int> when it calls biggest(3, 7).
**Before linking:** the linker will find the generated code, and the undefined reference disappears.

examples.title: The helper defined twice
examples.situation: A learner writes `int square(int x) { return x * x; }` in math.h, included by three .cpp files. Linking reports multiple definition of square.
walkthrough: Each unit compiled its own copy: three definitions.
Either mark it inline in the header,
or keep only the declaration in math.h and define it in math.cpp.
examples.result: One definition exists, and all three files use it.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: If separate .cpp files compile, declarations and definitions across them cannot violate a C++ program rule.
misconceptions.correction: Compilation checks one unit at a time. Missing, duplicate or mismatched definitions across units are only found at link time, and some ODR violations aren't diagnosed at all.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, which stage reported the problem?

analogy.example: A template is like **a cookie cutter**. You can only make star cookies (biggest<int>) in a kitchen that has the cutter. Keeping the cutter in one kitchen (util.cpp) means other kitchens can't make stars, and the bakery (linker) finds none when assembling the order.
usefulFor: remembering the cutter must be in the kitchen
limitations: Kitchens can copy cutters freely; headers copy templates freely.
Two different recipes with the same name is an ODR violation.

artifact: move template body to util.h; rebuild

steps.explanation: Each file compiles, but no unit generated biggest<int>.
The linker can't find the missing instantiation for int.
A template definition remains visible in a header so main.cpp can instantiate it.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a template link error. Step 1, Compile: main.o is needs biggest<int>; util.o is no instantiation. Each file compiles, but no unit generated biggest<int>. Step 2, Link: error is undefined reference. The linker can't find the missing instantiation for int. Step 3, Fix: util.h is full template; link is ok. A template definition remains visible in a header so main.cpp can instantiate it.

nearTransfer.prompt: Classify each error by stage and name the fix: (a) `fatal error: vectr: No such file`, (b) `no matching function for call to 'f(std::string)'`, (c) `undefined reference to 'Parser::run()'`, (d) `multiple definition of 'helper()'`.
scaffold: (c) often means a missing .cpp in the link.

farTransfer.prompt: Build a three-file program with one template and one ordinary helper. Reproduce each failure on purpose (template in .cpp, helper defined in header without inline, missing object in link), capture the messages, then fix all three.

remediation.explanation: Read the first error and ask: **file (preprocess), code (compile), or definition (link)?** For link errors, ask: **zero definitions or several?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The helper defined twice".

recap.summary: To classify and repair build failures, remember each .cpp is compiled separately and then linked, keep exactly one definition of each non-inline function and variable, define inline functions and templates in headers so every unit that uses them can see them, and read error wording to identify the stage.
